---
title: Chronological branches
description: "Ordered rows as time series: defaults, time, direction, masking, forecasting, per-row representations, and a contrastive objective."
engine: markdown
---

A time series is a [Branch](../datatypes/branch.qmd) whose rows have an order.
`rf.Branch.chronological(...)` builds a plain `Branch` with settings that suit
that order. Every setting also works on a plain `Branch`, and a saved model
stores the result as an ordinary `Branch`.

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    ett=rf.Branch.chronological(
        length=336,
        HUFL=rf.Number,
        OT=rf.Number,
    ),
)
```

## What the defaults change

| Option | `Branch(...)` | `Branch.chronological(...)` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `overflow` | `"head"` when `length` is set | `"tail"` when `length` is set: keep the latest rows |
| `grain` | `rf.Coordinates()` | `rf.Steps()` |
| `mixer` | `rf.Transformer()` | `rf.Conv()` |
| `direction` | `rf.Direction.bidirectional` | `rf.Direction.causal` |
| `time_index`, `time_step`, `contrastive` | `None` | `None` |

Each explicit argument replaces its default. The sections below explain what
each option does.

## Declare channels

Declare one `Number` per channel, or read all channels of a row as one
`Vector`:

```python
per_channel = rf.Branch.chronological(length=336, HUFL=rf.Number, HULL=rf.Number, OT=rf.Number)
per_row = rf.Branch.chronological(length=336, load=rf.Vector(query=("HUFL", "HULL", "OT")))
```

Separate `Number` fields keep a normalizer, a decoder, and a mask for each
channel, so a channel can be a target or a hidden input on its own. A `Vector`
is one field with one shared width: it suits channels that always travel
together, and a null in one source only marks that channel missing. See
[Vector](../datatypes/vector.qmd#channels-from-several-sources).

A branch reads each row as a struct. Dense `list<fixed_size_list<C>>` data has
no struct per row. Wrap each step in a `Preprocessor`, or read the whole run as
one [Series](../datatypes/series.qmd):

```python
import polars as pl


@rf.preprocess
def wrap(frame: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    step = pl.struct(pl.element().alias("load"))
    return frame.with_columns(pl.col("ett").list.eval(step))


rows = rf.Branch.chronological(length=336, load=rf.Vector(n_dim=7))
run = rf.Series(query="ett", n_dim=7)
```

See [query paths](../guides/query-paths.qmd#several-sources).

## Time

By default a row has the position of its count in the record. Name a leaf child
with `time_index` to give each row a position in time:

```python
import datetime

ett = rf.Branch.chronological(
    length=336,
    time_index="date",
    time_step=datetime.timedelta(hours=1),
    date=rf.Period("hour_of_day", "day_of_week"),
    OT=rf.Number,
)
```

- `time_index` names a direct leaf child. It stays an ordinary field, so a
  `Period` or a `Number` still embeds the same value.
- `time_step` is the unit of the positions: a `timedelta` for temporal columns,
  a number for numeric ones. It sets positions only and does not resample.
- Positions are relative to the first row of each record, may be real numbers,
  and must not decrease. Sorting belongs in a
  [preprocessor](../guides/preprocessing.qmd).
- A temporal `time_index` without `time_step` raises when the first batch is
  encoded, because the schema does not see the column type.

With `time_index`, each row token also receives a learned embedding of the time
since the previous row, in `time_step` units, before any mixer; the first row
gets zero. A convolution assumes evenly spaced rows, so without this embedding
`rf.Conv` would ignore irregular time. Attention reads the real positions as
well. A branch without `time_index` adds no parameters for time.

## Direction

::: {.callout-warning}
## Classification needs `direction=rf.Direction.bidirectional`

The causal default lets each step see only the steps at or before it. That is
right for forecasting and for per-step representations, and it discards the
future context a classifier should use. Causal is measured by step, not by
token: tokens of one step still see each other.
:::

UCR [GunPoint](https://timeseriesclassification.com/description.php?Dataset=GunPoint)
is a binary hand-motion task. Its 50 training and 150 test records each contain
one 150-step series; class `1` is gun-draw and class `2` is pointing. The UCR TSV
files store label in first column and 150 readings in remaining columns.

```python
import polars as pl
import relflow as rf


def gunpoint(path: str) -> pl.DataFrame:
    wide = pl.read_csv(path, separator="\t", has_header=False)
    steps = wide.columns[1:]
    return wide.select(
        pl.col("column_1").cast(pl.String).alias("label"),
        pl.concat_list(
            *(pl.struct(pl.col(name).alias("value")) for name in steps)
        ).alias("signal"),
    )


training = gunpoint("data/GunPoint_TRAIN.tsv").sample(fraction=1.0, shuffle=True, seed=0)
train, validate = training.head(40), training.tail(10)
test = gunpoint("data/GunPoint_TEST.tsv")

model = rf.Model.xs(
    label=rf.Category(mask=True),
    signal=rf.Branch.chronological(
        length=150,
        direction=rf.Direction.bidirectional,
        value=rf.Number,
    ),
)
data = rf.PolarsDataModule(
    train=train,
    validate=validate,
    num_workers=0,
    persistent_workers=False,
    pin_memory=False,
)
model.fit(data, batch_size=16, max_epochs=30)

predicted = model.predict(test.drop("label"))
guess = predicted["predictions"].struct.field("label").struct.field("content").struct.field("value")
accuracy = (guess == test["label"]).mean()
```

The validation rows come only from the official training split. Keep the official
test split for final scoring. `accuracy` compares predicted labels with those
held-out answers.

`direction=` is accepted on child branches only; the generated root has no
direction. Use `rf.Direction.causal` with forecasting.

## Grain and mixer

`grain` decides what one token of the branch sequence stands for, and `mixer`
decides how those tokens mix.

| Option | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `grain` | `rf.Coordinates()` | One token per leaf coordinate of every row. |
| `grain` | `rf.Steps()` | One token per row. `Steps(pooling="query")` pools the leaves with a learned query; `pooling="mean"` averages them. |
| `mixer` | `rf.Transformer()` | Rotary self-attention layers. |
| `mixer` | `rf.Conv(n_blocks=6)` | Dilated convolution blocks. Each step feature sees `1 + 4*(2^n_blocks - 1)` steps: 253 at the default of six. |
| `mixer` | `None` | No sequence mixing; coordinate attention remains. |

For 336 rows and 7 channels, `Coordinates` gives the sequence encoder 2352
tokens and `Steps` gives 336. The test
`test_steps_sequence_tokens_measured_at_336_rows_and_7_channels` asserts both
numbers. Attention cost grows with the square of that width.

Leaves under `Steps` read only the token of their own row, so a decoder never
reads a later row through pooling. `rf.Conv()` requires `grain=rf.Steps()`, and
`rf.Steps()` rejects a child branch with `reduction=None`.

## Mask whole rows

`rf.Mask(select=...)` hides rows of a branch instead of coordinates chosen by a
rate or a query:

```python
spans = rf.Mask(select=rf.Spans(rate=0.15, length=8), reconstruct=True)
last_day = rf.Mask(select=rf.Forecast(horizon=24, targets=("OT",)), reconstruct=True)
```

- `select` cannot be combined with `query` or `rate` in the same `Mask`. A tuple
  of masks hides the union of its selections.
- `select` on a leaf raises; set it on a branch.
- `Spans` hides about `rate` of the rows in runs of `length`, every child of a
  hidden row included, nested collections too. It applies in training only.
  With `reconstruct=True` the hidden values become targets, which makes
  masked-row pretraining.
- A branch holds at most one `Forecast`.

See [Masking and reconstruction](masking-and-reconstruction.qmd).

## Forecast

Past target values stay visible, so `OT` is an ordinary input child. Never write
`OT=rf.Number(mask=True)` here: `mask=True` means `skip=True`, so `OT` would
never be embedded.

```python
ett = rf.Branch.chronological(
    length=336,
    time_index="date",
    time_step=datetime.timedelta(hours=1),
    mask=rf.Mask(select=rf.Forecast(horizon=24, targets=("OT",)), reconstruct=True),
    date=rf.Period("hour_of_day", "day_of_week"),
    HUFL=rf.Number,
    OT=rf.Number,
)
```

- `Forecast(horizon=k, targets=(...), known=(...))` hides every child except the
  `time_index` child and the `known` children in the last `k` rows, nested
  branches included. Only the hidden `targets` become reconstruction targets;
  other hidden children are inputs only.
- `targets` and `known` name direct leaf children, never the `time_index` child,
  and must not overlap. Use `known` for covariates available in advance, such
  as calendar fields or planned prices.
- The mask needs `reconstruct=True` and rejects `skip=True`. `Forecast` needs
  `direction=rf.Direction.causal`, and the `time_index` child must read a single
  member.
- `length` is the context. Training, validation, and test read `length +
  horizon` rows; prediction reads `length` rows.

At prediction a future row is a trailing row in which every target child is
null.

- A record with any future row gets no automatic rows. More than `horizon`
  future rows raise.
- Otherwise `k` rows are appended and fill only the `time_index` child. This
  matches training only when `known` is empty, so a branch with `known`
  covariates raises with the `known` names unless you supply future rows.
- Non-known children in future rows are hidden whatever they hold.

Supply future rows with the known values and null targets in a preprocessor:

```python
@rf.preprocess
def extend(frame: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    future = pl.datetime_ranges(
        pl.col("last_date") + pl.duration(hours=1),
        pl.col("last_date") + pl.duration(hours=24),
        interval="1h",
    )
    return frame.with_columns(
        ett=pl.concat_list(
            pl.col("ett"),
            future.list.eval(pl.struct(date=pl.element(), OT=pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.Float64))),
        )
    )
```

Here `frame` has a `last_date` column holding the final observed time of each record. A missing `known` column at prediction raises `MissingFieldError`. Predicted
rows appear as ordinary rows of the branch list in the output, and each carries
`inferred` in its leaf result.

## Representations

A reduction passes `K` summaries per record to the parent. To keep one vector
per row, set `reduction=None` and use `rf.Steps()`, then `embed=True`:

```python
rows = rf.Branch.chronological(length=336, reduction=None, embed=True, HUFL=rf.Number, OT=rf.Number)
```

The prediction output then holds one representation per row: `path` names the
branch, `parents` ends with the row ordinal, and `output_index` is `0`. With the
causal default, the vector of row `t` depends on rows up to `t` only. Under
`rf.Coordinates()` a branch keeps one representation per token, as before. See
[Prediction output](../reference/prediction-output.qmd#representations) and
[Branch summaries](branch-summaries.qmd).

## Contrastive pretraining

`contrastive` adds a training objective that needs no labels:

```python
rows = rf.Branch.chronological(
    length=336,
    contrastive=rf.Contrastive(views=rf.Crops(width=128, overlap=0.5), loss=rf.Hierarchical(), weight=1.0),
    HUFL=rf.Number,
    OT=rf.Number,
)
```

Each record yields two crops of `width` rows that share a fraction `overlap`.
The loss pulls matching rows of the two crops together, pushes apart rows of
other records and other rows of the same record, and repeats at coarser time
scales. Records shorter than `width` are masked, not padded with data.

- It runs in training only. The decoders and the parent still see the full
  record.
- It costs about three times the memory and compute of the branch, because two
  crops are encoded in addition to the full record.
- It rejects a child branch with `reduction=None`.
- Under distributed training, records are compared within the batch of each
  device only.
- A model whose only objective is contrastive logs no `loss/validate`, so pass
  `early_stopping=False, rollback=False` to `fit`, or add a reconstruction
  target.

## Name clashes

`grain`, `mixer`, `direction`, `time_index`, `time_step`, and `contrastive` are
`Branch` options. A child with one of these names goes in `fields`:

```python
rf.Branch(direction=rf.Direction.causal, fields={"direction": rf.Category})
```

Next, read the [Branch reference](../datatypes/branch.qmd#options) and
[Series](../datatypes/series.qmd).
